summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. Homosexuality carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995, and no equivalent provision has been reinstated since.

The operative instrument is the comprehensive anti-discrimination law in force from 4 February 2010, which covers sexual orientation in employment, goods and services, education, housing and health care, and which was expanded in October 2020 to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sex characteristics and HIV status.

Enforcement of that law is uneven. In December 2010 the Deputy Commissioner for Labour, Social Affairs and Health, Tritan Shehu, stated publicly that homosexuality should be treated by medical staff as a hormonal and psychological disorder; the Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination reprimanded him only on 30 September 2011, after a lengthy delay. LGBT groups had by then lost confidence in the body over slow and bureaucratically impeded investigations, with only one of nine LGBT-linked cases concluded by December 2012. A more recent test was the 2023 complaint over screenings of the film 'Strange World', which the Commissioner mediated with a ruling in favour of the complainant in one case.

Hate-motivated offences were placed on a statutory footing on 4 May 2013, when Parliament amended the criminal code to treat offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity on a par with offences motivated by race, ethnicity, religion or disability. The package adopted the same day also provides for a fine and up to two years' imprisonment for disseminating homophobic information through any means, including the internet.

The constitutional layer is weaker. In 2016, under pressure from faith-based leaders, members of parliament removed sexual orientation and gender identity from Article 18 of the Constitution at the last moment, contrary to earlier promises; PINK Embassy condemned the removal on 20 July 2016.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for same-sex marriage in July 2009, framing the question as part of EU integration, but no recognition followed.

Violence remains documented. For 2023, the ILGA-Europe Annual Review recorded ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people logged by the group Rainbowphilia. Community organisations ran support schemes in the same period, including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

Access to care is constrained by public attitudes as well as by the law. A 2022 nationwide questionnaire found that only 9.3% of Albanians would accept an LGBT person as a family doctor. Social hostility is also recorded in wider survey data: 56.1% of Albanians told Gallup's Balkan Monitor in 2010 that homosexuals should not show their preferences in public, and 56.2% said they should not hold public posts such as teacher; 55% of Albanians aged 16–27 said in 2015 that they would not want homosexual neighbours, and a 2016 study found homophobia among university students associated with being male, politically conservative and religious.

Official hostility surfaces in parliamentary speech. In October 2011 the Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu for telling parliament that 'homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones', warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community. In July 2021, during a row over LGBT campaigning in high schools, MP Luçiano Boçi attacked the groups as extra-curricular organisations with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda', while MP Nard Ndoka used Facebook to brand the government 'LGBT' and accuse it of pushing LGBT values in schools.

Schools policy has been a site of contention: in June 2016 the government passed a National Action Plan for LGBTI addressing bullying and discrimination in primary and secondary education, which drew strong political opposition.

The international review baseline is the visit of the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity to Albania from 1 to 12 July 2024, whose end-of-mission statement assessed good practices and challenges and set out recommendations to the State. The full report, A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 of 17 June 2025 by Independent Expert Graeme Reid, evaluates Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on sexual orientation and gender identity, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit.
tangentialFactors:
Public visibility efforts persist despite the attitudes recorded in survey data. Pro LGBT launched the news portal historiaime.al in 2012, and the first Miss Trans Albania pageant was held in Tirana in 2014.

Political framing of LGBT policy is frequently tied to European integration. The 2010 anti-discrimination law was presented in those terms by the government of the day, while opposition messaging in 2021 cast school-level LGBT education work as an imported agenda.

Albania's record compares favourably with jurisdictions in the region that retain criminal penalties for same-sex conduct, but its enforcement record and constitutional rollback distinguish it from states where equality guarantees have been strengthened over the same period.

Discrimination complaints in the cultural sector are handled through mediation before the Commissioner rather than through the courts, a route that produced a favourable ruling in one of the 'Strange World' screening cases without establishing a wider precedent.
localsOnly:
Residents can invoke the 2010 anti-discrimination law and its 2020 extension across employment, goods and services, education, housing, health care, sex characteristics and HIV status, and can lodge complaints with the Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination, though LGBT groups have documented slow and bureaucratically impeded handling of such files.

Constitutional protection is absent following the 2016 removal of sexual orientation and gender identity from Article 18, so residents have no constitutional ground of that kind to rely on.

Community infrastructure includes support schemes such as food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV, logging of bias-motivated violence by Rainbowphilia, and the Pro LGBT news portal historiaime.al.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Albania has a legal procedure for gender recognition, and how identity documents are handled after a gender change, is unresolved in the available material: the People's Advocate, Erinda Ballanca, pledged in April 2018 to support the right to legally change one's gender, but no source in this inventory states whether such a procedure exists, what it requires, or how markers are issued.

No sourced information covers airport or border screening practices, custody or detention placement by gender marker, or access to hormone therapy for visitors; these remain not sourced rather than established as absent.

Bathroom and facilities rules, and any trans-specific provisions in policing or hate-crime prosecution statistics beyond the ten cases logged by Rainbowphilia for 2023, are not sourced here.

The ten-year penalty that applied until 1995 and the 2013 homophobic-materials offence are described from secondary summaries; the operative wording of the current criminal code provisions is not directly quoted in this inventory.
